17001:
Kevin already got an answer from Ken about some of the changes that he will see between "AstroBASIC" games that have been updated to use under Expanded BASIC (namely, ViperSoft BASIC, Blue Ram BASIC and Hot Rod BASIC-- am I missing any of these upgraded BASIC languages?).

An Expanded BASIC user will get more colors.  Usually this is four colors compared to two colors of just the foreground and background allowed under normal circumstance in Bally BASIC).  If the screen is split, then you'd get up to four colors vs. "AstroBASIC's" four colors.

A user of Expanded BASIC also get better animation.  This is because of Expanded BASIC's ability to not store the BASIC program in screen RAM (which allows for additional colors), but this also has the positive side affect of allowing programs to run faster because programs don't have to be packed and unpacked from screen RAM.  This make a huge difference in program execution speed.

Expanded BASIC has the PLAY command which is used to directly access the music routines in the on-board ROM.  A program that uses the PLAY possibly can have access to music being played while a program is running.  George Moses wrote an article about this for the Arcadian in 1983:

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/PLAY%20Command%20Tutorial/How%20to%20Use%20the%20Blue%20Ram%20Basic%20PLAY%20Command%20-%20A%20Tutorial%20(George%20Moses)(Arcadian,%20June%20and%20August%201983).pdf

Two games where you'll see big differences between the AstroBASIC and Blue Ram BASIC releases are WaveMakers' "The Gate Escape" and "Outpost 19."  In both cases the games look and sound better when run under Expanded BASIC, but-- not to be negative-- the games are still basically the same in both cases.  In fact, I prefer the simpler graphics of the AstroBASIC version of "Outpost 19" to the expanded BASIC's much-improved graphics.

In the days of the Astrocade newsletters, the Expanded BASIC programs were usually said to be something that might have been released on cartridge.  I wouldn't go that far; the movement in the games is nearly as fluid of machine language programs... and yet, games that don't require fast action can look (but not quite act) just like a game released on cartridge.  However, that's only if just BASIC is used for animation.  If a Blue Ram BASIC game uses machine language routines, then I've no doubt that it probably could be just as fast and smooth as a game released on cartridge.

Expanded BASIC has access to far more RAM than ROM cartridges.  Although the 4K of the RAM of the Astrocade is highly touted, even cartridges are limited to usually just a few hundred usable bytes at the bottom of the screen.  A good example of a game where you can "see" the RAM being used is "Amazing Maze."  In that game, when the maze is being generated, the bottom of the screen seems to get "garbage" spewed all about it.  This is because the cartridge requires more RAM to create the maze; an Expanded BASIC program wouldn't be required to use screen RAM, so this "thinking" that the program is doing when the maze is generated would not need to be shown on-screen.

Now that I've written this overly-long post, which probably only scratches the surface of the advantages of the Expanded BASICs, it makes me wonder how many AstroBASIC games were converted to use expanded BASIC?  Is anyone up for making a video comparison of some of these games?

Adam

“A Study of 4D Julia sets” is a ray traced abstract mathematical animation of fractal forms created by iterating the equation z = z^2 +k in the 4 dimensional quaternion number system. The concepts are an extension of the iterations in complex numbers. In complex numbers create 2 dimensional forms. These same iterations in the quaternion number system produce 4 dimensional forms. Supplying K, a 4 dimensional vector, specifies the entire variety of forms in the work. The resulting 4D form is sectioned down to 3 dimensions. The Ray tracing method was developed by John Hart and presented at SIGGRAPH 1989. The rest of the fun is lighting, timing, camera control and music.

17013:
Last Friday I had a lengthy phone conversation with Tom Meeks, who worked at Astrocade in the early 80s. Years back he had a nice back-and-forth in this group, and in some regards our conversation was a follow up to that. I'm still going through my notes/refining them with the transcription, but Tom said he had no problem with me sharing his recollections with other interested parties, so I thought I'd share some highlights.
On coming to Astrocade: Tom was a video production guy and a part time teacher when he got the Astrocade job. He had bought the system around 1979 when he realized it put out a broadcast-quality signal, and messed around with the original BASIC cart. Tom also owned a Datamax UV1 due to his video production work, and eventually got in touch with a local Astrocade distributor to talk shop - this led to him getting a job interview with the company and a job, working under the sales manager, Ray George. With the company, Meeks described himself as "chief Galaxian killer." He was based out of Maryland - working out of his home until Astrocade paid up for a temp office in the area - but would fly across the country to assist with demonstrations. He'd be the one showing off their games and the hardware and what one could do with it, explaining why it was better than Atari and Mattel's consoles, and helping local reps learn how to sell it. 
The other part of his job involved meeting up with Dave Nutting and Bob Ogden's crew in Chicago about every Friday to talk about software: testing games, getting feedback from enthusiasts and public testers and using that to tweak the games. Dave Nutting Associates was still in charge of software, but they were open to outside ideas and suggestions. Meeks was also involved with the ZGRASS add-on, helping design the keyboard interface and even drawing up a design for a graphics tablet that would connect to it - at the time a high end input device. His design involved it being integrated into the keyboard, though since it would have dramatically driven up the price he understands why this was not pursued.
On the add-on: I asked Tom how the ZGRASS expansion compared to the UV1. He said the biggest difference was speed. Because the UV1 used a higher clocked Z80 processor, didn't have to share memory and screen time with the Astrocade, and could be upgraded with even more memory, the UV1 was fast. The add-on, on the other hand, could see the animation bogged down. ZGRASS itself worked incredibly well for getting what you wanted done, but compared to machine language it was a slower effort. This actually matches up with something another historian, Alex Smith, heard from Jamie Fenton last year in an interview - Fenton said she originally liked ZGRASS in the add-on, but eventually turned on it because it was too slow and she's all about speed. One revision of the add on used Forth, she told Smith, which was much quicker (but clearly not what DNA was showing to Astrocade). Jim McConnell, Astrocade's hardware engineer, worked closely with the DNA folks - Tom said Jim also designed the 2000-baud cassette interface for AstroBASIC. 
On the work environment at Astrocade: Meeks painted a picture of a fairly political company that was divided into two camps and several strata. Ray George and Jim Guerin, who had worked together to scoop up the Bally system after struggling to get their own home game product off the ground. Jim ran the business side of things, and Ray the sales side. Tom had very little experience with Jim's team but noted that Ray was an "intimidating" salesman who was also charismatic enough that even a room full of pissed off reps and distributors would be happy to buy more product after meeting with him. He didn't feel Ray had a whole lot of interest in the product other than being something to sell, but the folks on his own stratum - Jim McConnell, himself, and the Dave Nutting folks - were all big believers in the product and felt it was better than the competitors' machines. he also suspects Ray and/or his sales team had some messed up payment arrangement that they were gaming the system with: to explain, Ray would get a commission for new sales and a different commission for selling product generally to existing reps. So he would recruit representatives and distributors, having Tom wow them with their games and quality, and then provide them with mostly mediocre games and a smattering of good ones to get into stores. As Tom said, you can't sell consoles without the good games, and when those reps failed to live up to their contracts to move product, Ray could break it, find another potential local rep in the same area, and get them on board with the same scam. He's not sure if this was Ray George specifically or someone on the sales team doing it or everybody, but he said it seemed counterproductive towards success. 
Furthermore, Guerin and George did not like each other, and as the animosity built up Guerin founded Nitron to actually build the Astrocades. The setup was that Astrocade would get an order in, they'd get the money, and then it would go into a "lockbox" and move on to Nitron to pay for the production. If Astrocade failed to pay, Nitron would take over the company (and thus cut George out entirely). So there were some efforts around this time to get the product sold off to another company or find some other solution to keep Nitron from taking over. Meeks said they had a meeting with Fisher Price, which was very interested and tentatively offered $3 million to buy out Astrocade and the game system. Around this time they also got a lead that Hasbro was interested, and similarly Hasbro offered them $3 million as well, Meeks said. Ray George, trying to play them off each other, told Hasbro they appreciated it, but that they already had this tentative deal with Fisher Price. Hasbro's folks didn't appreciate going through this demo and song and dance when a tentative offer already existed and dropped out. Then an enthusiast caught wind of the potential sale, reached out to Fisher Price to congratulate them on going after the Astrocade, and inadvertently killed that deal as FP didn't want to deal with a company with that kind of leaking going on.
The death of Astrocade: Meeks recounted the tale of what really ended up doing Astrocade in. He and Ray George were in Europe after that went down trying to drum up a distributor out there who could financially help them keep Nitron from taking over the company. And they found a West German guy who was interested, provided they could design a PAL Astrocade unit (which finally pushed Jeff Fredricksen to do so). The German fellow was willing to pay handsomely to become the European distributor for the product, ITT was going to produce the units, everything was looking good. Well Tom says that Ray George had this "disgusting friend" there with them, and after they got the commitment from the distributor, this fellow calls New York Post financial reporter Dan Dorfman and tells him that Nitron is going to have some trouble because Astrocade can't pay them, and that this may end up being illegal. He then hangs up and says that it should keep Nitron busy for a while and should keep them from taking over Astrocade until they get the money from the German fellow. Well, flash forward a little bit - Ray George has set up this meeting with a big investment bank in New York and the German guy is coming in to give him the check and sign the formal paperwork: George thinks doing this with the investment bankers will make everything seem more impressive all around. He finishes his presentation, Tom does his part, and one of the investment bankers says this all looks good and they don't care what Dan Dorfman said in the paper that day. Well, no one at Astrocade nor the German guy had seen this, so the German guy goes downstairs, buys the paper, comes back up and reads the piece blasting Ray George and company as being disreputable. Tom recalls the guy's face turned beet red, that he took the check and put it back in his coat pocket, asked for a cab to be called, and left. And once he left, the investment bankers were no longer interested in the product, either. To quote "They outsmarted themselves."
Odds and ends: Tom wasn't around for the Bally sell off to Astrocade, but heard secondhand that Bally cut the home division loose in part because it was underperforming and in part because they were under investigation for mob ties and, because it was underperforming, the folks in charge were fingered and the division sold off. Bally itself had no experience selling on the consumer market and didn't seem to understand how to market the machine.
After Astrocade laid folks off and filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy (Tom remembers being at CES during that taking place when they were named a #1 company by Consumer Reports), Tom worked for a couple local publishers making computer software, which eventually led to his program Homework Helper getting sold off to Spinnaker. He was involved with the Mindset computer after realizing its potential for video production, and his production software was even packed in with the machine for a time (it ultimately went under in part because of problems getting the hard drive to work). I can get into more detail on Mindset if there's interest. He also worked with John Perkins on Project NEMO - the game system Hasbro financially backed that could play games off VHS tapes - and gives Perkins 100% credit for solving the multiple video stream problem they faced.

17033:
Kevin asked how to remove the Lil' White RAM from the back of the Astrocade.  It's a good question, as the RAM unit is very difficult to take off once it's on the Astrocade.  This is because, unlike a cartridge, which has the male edge connector inside of it, the Astrocade's 50-pin connector (which is used for upgrades like those required for RAM expansions) is made up of part of the motherboard.

The RAM expansion units on the astrocade have a female edge connector.  Since contact the motherboard is very important, to avoid signal noise, these connectors must be very tight to allow the signal to pass through between the Z80 and the external hardware expansion.  If the connectors were not tight, then RAM expansions on the astrocade would have similar problems to the RAM expansions for the Timex Sinclair computers: a slight wobble of the expansion would crash the system.  Luckily, the infamous "wobble" of the Timex Sinclair 1000 doesn't occur on the astrocade because the connections are tight.

The simple answer for how to remove the RAM expansion from an Astrocade isn't one that you will like to hear: remove it very carefully.  With this statement, I am not trying to be funny or obnoxious, although it does come across that way.

When Paul Thacker, Ken Lill and I met at the Louisville Arcade Expo in 2016, Paul asked Ken what the best way was to remove the RAM expansion from the astrocade.  Even carefully trying to remove the unit doesn't work very well.  In the end, you'll probably find that removing the hardware upgrade from the Astrocade 50-pin connector is probably best done, as Ken suggested at the show, with the astrocade's top cover removed.  This is the way that I do it.  However, for me, this is easy because I only use my astrocade with its RF shield and its cover removed.  I gently wiggle the expansion back and forth, slowly and carefully, until it is completely removed from the astrocade's motherboard.  This was difficult to accomplish in the early days of owning the unit, but now I can remove it pretty easily.

As far as using the Lil' White RAM without power supply to the unit, I do this when I use the 300-BAUD interface.  It hasn't caused me any issues.  However, I wasn't aware (or maybe I forgot) that you are not supposed to do this for some reason.  I would like see Ken weigh in on this matter.  Also, I think the newest Lil' White RAM units are powered by USB connectors.  Or, at least that was the plan for newly-made units.  I'm not sure if these units have been made yet.

I want to clear-up that the tight connection between the Lil' White RAM and the astrocade is not a fault of the design.  Nor, is this "feature" limited to just the expansion created by Ken and Mike White.  The Blue Ram and Viper expansions also have this issue.  Please, don't let this issue distract anyone from using or owning one of these upgrades, as they are extremely useful and are fun to use.

Adam

The simple answer for how to remove the RAM expansion from an Astrocade isn't one that you will like to hear: remove it very carefully.  With this statement, I am not trying to be funny or obnoxious, although it does come across that way.

When Paul Thacker, Ken Lill and I met at the Louisville Arcade Expo in 2016, Paul asked Ken what the best way was to remove the RAM expansion from the astrocade.  Even carefully trying to remove the unit doesn't work very well.  In the end, you'll probably find that removing the hardware upgrade from the Astrocade 50-pin connector is probably best done, as Ken suggested at the show, with the astrocade's top cover removed.  This is the way that I do it.  However, for me, this is easy because I only use my astrocade with its RF shield and its cover removed.  I gently wiggle the expansion back and forth, slowly and carefully, until it is completely removed from the astrocade's motherboard.  This was difficult to accomplish in the early days of owning the unit, but now I can remove it pretty easily.

As far as using the Lil' White RAM without power supply to the unit, I do this when I use the 300-BAUD interface.  It hasn't caused me any issues.  However, I wasn't aware (or maybe I forgot) that you are not supposed to do this for some reason.  I would like see Ken weigh in on this matter.  Also, I think the newest Lil' White RAM units are powered by USB connectors.  Or, at least that was the plan for newly-made units.  I'm not sure if these units have been made yet.

I want to clear-up that the tight connection between the Lil' White RAM and the astrocade is not a fault of the design.  Nor, is this "feature" limited to just the expansion created by Ken and Mike White.  The Blue Ram and Viper expansions also have this issue.  Please, don't let this issue distract anyone from using or owning one of these upgrades, as they are extremely useful and are fun to use.

Adam

Kevin is planning to use his 300-BAUD BASIC interface with Bally BASIC.  It would be great if he could make some videos of some of the programs that he loads.  There are precious few videos of anyone using that method to load tapes.

I think that people often misunderstand, or maybe they just forget, that for three years (1978-1981) the only way to load and save BASIC programs on the Bally Arcade was to use the separate 300-baud tape interface with Bally BASIC.  When I initially used BASIC on the Astrocade, I used "AstroBASIC" first and it was hard for me to step back to the earlier version of Bally BASIC because the loading time of about three minutes to input a 1.8K program seemed overly long.  Really though, it's only three minutes, which isn't a long time at all.  We're just used to instant-loading via cartridges on older systems.

An example of BASIC programs mostly-only available in 300-BAUD format are programs by Seebree's Computing:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Sebrees_Computing/Sebrees_Computing.html

Heck, some of their programs are not available in any format.  Maybe someone can type a few of them into BASIC:

Hit the Pedestrian:

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/sebree/hit_the_pedestrian.pdf

Munch:

https://ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/sebree/munch.pdf

The Bally BASIC programs that didn't get changed over the "AstroBASIC" format are often simpler than later programs.  Using and playing Bally BASIC program is an excellent way to see what most programs and games were like before "AstroBASIC" allowed people to work and program with more speed and also with the ability to edit programs more easily.

If anyone, not just Kevin, made some videos of using 300-Baud programs with Bally BASIC, then that would be great!

Adam

Once there are a few people who come forward to say they will work on an "AstroBASIC" game and I can put out some general rules.  For now, just keep these not written-in- stone in mind:

1) The program must be written for "AstroBASIC" - Loading and saving with Bally BASIC isn't supported with the MAME emulator.  Using "AstroBASIC" allows everyone to program in the same version of BASIC.

2) The BASIC program and any machine language subroutines must fit into 1.8K of RAM - AstroBASIC" doesn't directly allow access to more 1.8K of RAM, but I think there are ways around it using some tricks.

3) Ports and Originals - I prefer to see people making original games, but if someone wants to go ahead and port a game from any era and from any platform to "AstroBASIC," then that is fine with me.

These aren't really the official rules, and honestly, this is just a "competition" in the loosest form of the term.  Honestly, I find investigating and possibly writing a game in "AstroBASIC" fun.  I know myself pretty well and I expect that if left to my own devices, then I'd never finish a game.  However, with some limitations set, such as an end-date, then I might actually finish a game of some sort.

17065:
The main trouble with the MLM is that, for the most part, it "only" supports the 300-baud interface.  The old tape interface isn't supported in MAME.  It's true that the MLM can be forced to use the 2000-baud interface via cartridge swapping.  This works with real hardware, but cartridge swapping is also not supported in MAME.  Plus, on the best of days, cartridge swapping on a real astrocade is pretty finicky.  Once you get the method down, it works okay, but it's a bit of trail and error at first.  Certainly I would never want to trust saving my machine language program that I typed in using the 24-key keypad to tape using the cart-swap method.

If you're going to write a program using the MLM over "AstroBASIC," then you're writing in machine language.  In this case, you probably might want to switch to using a cross assembler to create your Z80 code and then make a cartridge for the Astrocade.  There are actually some advantages to using the MLM compared to a cross-assembler (like Zmac).  For instance, you get immediate feedback, you can check the registers easily, and the MLM takes care of some of the dirty work for the programmer.

For me, for this challenge, I like the idea of programming in Bally BASIC (or "AstroBASIC"), as nearly all of the programs in the Astrocade newsletters and the programs on tapes were written in that language.  Sure, it has severe limitations, but people dealt with them in the 1970s/1980s.  I guess we can deal with them now.  Plus, it might be fun to work around those limitations as many of the programmers did in the later era of "AstroBASIC" programming.

The main advantage of BASIC for most microcomputers is that I suspect that someone with absolutely no programming knowledge could pick up the "AstroBASIC" manual, read and follow all of the examples in the book and then this newly-hatched programmer could understand how to program, to a limited extent, in just a few days.  That's just not going to happen with machine language.

Adam

Bally Arcade/Astrocade - Color Comparison in AstroBASIC
Real Hardware vs. MAME
By Adam Trionfo
April 20, 2020


Anyone who uses the Astrocade emulation in MAME is probably aware that the colors don't match up with real hardware properly.  Some colors are close, while others are WAY off what they should look like under emulation.  Some colors are completely wrong.

Since I have been programming in the last few days using AstroBASIC under MAME, this has become even more apparent (and annoying) to me.  A Bally BASIC programmer depends on the screen color because color changes made to the screen by one of the four shift keys must match the color of the key that is pressed on the 24-key keyboard overlay.  In a couple cases, the shift keys are completely wrong (for instance, the red shift key turns the screen yellow).

I made a side-by-side AstroBASIC screen comparison to make it easy for anyone to see the differences between the colors on real hardware and MAME.  I've made one picture that includes what the colors of the shift-word keys look like on a real astrocade next to colors as they are seen in MAME.  To make this easier to understand, each screenshot that I took explains what you're looking at on the screen.

I took screenshots of my CRT TV using my camera.  The colors are about accurate to how they look on my actual CRT.  The red is little off in the picture of my CRT (the CRT's screen is more red, not murky reddish-pink in the picture), but the camera's pictures are approximately right.  As you can see, the colors under MAME are sometimes close and sometimes not even in the same color range.

This posting should include an attachment that I'm sending to the Astrocade discussion at Groups.io.  I'd like to know that people can see it.  If you can't see it, then please tell me what you see in this posting in your email box.

Here is a breakdown of the color differences you'll see in the compilation of pictures, as seen from top to bottom:

1) AstroBASIC - Default Colors - B&W - MAME gets this about right.
2) AstroBASIC - Green Shift Key - MAME's shade of green is off, but at least it get the correct color.  It still should be adjusted in MAME.
3) AstroBASIC - Red Shift Key - MAME is completely wrong.  The screen should be red, but it is yellow-ish/gold instead.
4) AstroBASIC - Blue Shift Key - MAME is wrong here.  The sceen should be blue, but it is light-purple instead.
5) AstroBASIC - Words/Gold Shift Key - MAME's shade of "gold" is off (it's bright yellow), but at least it's in the same-ish color range.

I hope that this helps a programmer track down the issue that the Astrocade emulation in MAME has with displaying the correct colors.

Does anyone have any ideas on how these colors can be fixed in MAME?

Adam

17086:
The issue with MAME emulation is two-fold.  Because MAME strives for
accuracy...the custom ICs should be characterized correctly so that the
emulation generates a representation of the actual signal coming out of
it.  Then, for arcade systems...the effect of the RGB converter board and
monitor can be modelled as an additional effect for them.  And for the
Astrocade the effect of a TV can be handled seperately.

The scope allows one to seperate these effects.  Also...if anyone is ever
going to make replacements for the custom ICs...this analysis needs to be
done this way.

I wrote an AstroBASIC program called "All 256 Colors" using MAME.  It was inspired by "Color Wheel" from the "AstroBASIC" manual.  The program displays the background color in all 32 colors and 8 intensities (for a total of 256 colors).  Each screen displays the BASIC color (0-255), the Background Color 0-31 and the Background Intensity (0-7).  After each screen is displayed, there is a short pause before the program proceeds.  You may want to set NT=0 before the program starts, as it will run faster that way.

I'm most concerned that my program is displaying the right Color and Intensity values.  I think my program is accurate, but I'd like someone to at least look the code over and, even better, try it on real hardware.

I wrote "All 256 Colors" as a test program to help identify the color issues with MAME.  If the program is correct, then I'll make a video of it running using my Canon Camera.  The camera should get a good approximation of each color that is displayed on my CRT TV.  This way people who might attempt to fix MAME's color palette issue with the Astrocade emulation will have something to compare against the colors when displayed under Astrocade emulation in MAME.

Here is the first of the 256 screens that are created:

[cid:48f3745d-9390-438e-853d-4cfbc2ee5aa4]

Here is the last of the 256 screens that are created:

[cid:c3eefcca-36a1-4bf8-b523-541406572b42]

Here is a BASIC listing of the program which I obtained via MAME and tools like BallyBin.

5 CLEAR
10 FOR C=0TO 31
20 FOR I=0TO 7
30 BC=C×8+I
40 FC=BC+12
42 CLEAR
43 PRINT "BASIC COLOR   BC        BC"
45 PRINT "   NUMBER","  COLOR"," INTENSITY"
50 PRINT C×8+I,C,I
52 FOR A=0TO 2000;NEXT A
60 NEXT I
70 NEXT C

I've attached several files to this posting, including the 2000-baud WAV file of the program.  I output the AstroBASIC 2000-baud RAW file from MAME and then cleaned it with BallyBin and AstroWAV 1.4.  Remember, you can load this program in newer versions of MAME or you can use it on real hardware.

Can anyone help test this program and does anyone have any suggestions for it?

Adam

Computer Entertainer was also useful for the last few releases, as they kept track of new games coming out starting around September 1982 and were very quick to review titles. Beyond that though I had to basically work with what I could get out of old newspaper ads, and those are pretty generic early on for the Bally.
Brett, if you've got any ideas on when ICBM Attack came out I'd appreciate it, as that was one I had trouble getting a handle on. The list also should probably note that BASICarts started becoming available at the end there.
Combined with Mike White's thorough pdf on the website of cassette/type-in programs noting who wrote what and when it was published, I think we've got a largely complete picture of the Astrocade's world of releases.

Paul Thacker and I recorded Astrocast #14 on Thursday, March 12, 2020.  Chris finished editing the episode a little over a week ago and it has been ready to upload since that time.  I've been attempting to create the show notes and should be done soon.

Paul and I cover the October 1979 issue of the Arcadian along with sixteen documents from the Bob Fabris collection .  While the episode has not been edited yet, I finally collected all the documents together and uploaded them to archive.org as PDF files.  These files have still not been added to ballyalley.com, and they not may not make it there anytime soon.

You can view and download the sixteen documents, here:

https://archive.org/details/Bally_Astrocade_Document_Collection_Astrocast_14/mode/1up

I hope to upload Astrocast #14 by tomorrow.

Here is my full description of the documents that I added today.  Check 'em out and enjoy 'em.  Reading this correspondence to Bob Fabris helps to bring illumination to the Bally Arcade scene as it stood in about October 1979.

Adam

Bally Arcade/Astrocade
Document Collection for Astrocast #14
Collected by Adam Trionfo
April 27, 2020


These are sixteen letters, postcards, notes and even one telegram that were sent to Bob Fabris, editor of the Arcadian newsletter, in the late 1970s/early 1980s.  These letters are covered by Paul Thacker and Adam Trionfo, the hosts of the Bally Alley Astrocast, in podcast #14.  The Astrocast covers the Bally Arcade/Astrocade, a game console released in 1978.

You can listen to the podcast here:

http://ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/podcast

These documents are in pdf format.  Those that were typed have been OCRed but several of these documents are handwritten, so character recognition was not possible.  There is a wealth of information inside of these documents which have been scanned from the Bob Fabris Collection.  Names of the document are listed here, along with extremely terse overviews about what is in some the documents.  The only way to really know what is inside of these documents is to dig into them and read them from start to finish.

The sixteen documents are:

Letter to Bob Fabris (1982)(Lindsay Olsen)(Help with Microtrek).pdf - September 28, 1982.  Needs help with Microtrek by Bill Andrus.  Telegram

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 27 1979)(Brett Bilbrey).pdf - October 27, 1979. University of Michigan in the Office of Individualized Learning. Bally User Group. TRS-80. Compucolor, Life, Dr. Zinn, Creative Computing.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Frank Gfelner)(Oct 14 1979)(VideoBrain Keyboard).pdf - October 14, 1979. Ram upgrade and VideoBrain keyboard.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Nov 21 1979)(Ed Mulholland).pdf -  Postcard.  November 21, 1979. Error with Resequencing by Ron Schweitzer.  Jerry Tindle. Keyboard upgrade.

Arcadian - 10 Programs (Permission Form)(William Andrus).pdf - June 30, 1981. Arcadian - 10 Programs compilation. Signed Microtrek Permission Form.

Letter to Bob Fabris (HO Meyers)(Oct 12 1979).pdf - October 12, 1979. Bill Kopp. Overheating. $35 Bally board replacement.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 14 1979)(Harry Hanson).pdf - October 14, 1979. Postcard.  Discouragement with Bally. A fading Bally Buff.  "Thrown out unit long ago!"

Letter to Bob Fabris (Robert Lilly)(Oct 15 1979).pdf - October 15, 1979. Survey Response. Checkers bug. Heathkit H-8. Heathkit H-11a.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 15 1979)(Bernard Haberman).pdf - October 15, 1979. Survery Response. Montgomery Ward unit. Failed unit. Checkers error or bug. Serial Number 8,845.

Letter to Bob Fabris (George Tucker)(Oct 16 1979).pdf - October 16, 1979.  Letter with a short, 4-line BASIC program that makes a gunshot.  ZGrass.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 18 1979)(Stuart Zolten)(DigiTrends).pdf - October 18, 1979. Digitrends, Inc from Cleveland, Ohio. Carries Bally software and hardware. Mentions the Mattel Intellivision keyboard.

Concentration - Division - Hex Dump (October 20 1979)(Anson Winsor)(BASIC Listings).pdf - October 20, 1979. A four-page, typed letter with explanations and information about the 6 pages of handwritten BASIC listings for three programs: Concentration, Division to "N" Decimal Places and Hex Dump.  These programs were never published in the Arcadian.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 22 1979)(Phil Shafer).pdf - October 22, 1979. New cartridge releases.  PA-1 Service Manual. Executive Manual.  Space Invaders and Bally Pin will be out soon.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Herb Weintraub)(Oct 24 1979).pdf - October 24, 1979.  Short program that is a variation of the Arcadian program on page 57. Classified Ad. Wanted business programs written for a small quick printer. Instant printing.  This letter is addressed to: Robert Fabris, Staff, Boss, Proofreader, Stapler, folder, stamp licker, typist.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Oct 29 1979)(Larry Schmitt).pdf - October 29, 1979. Bally Arcade used as a premium and gift. Disappointment with Bally promotion and advertisements. Bally Buffs.  Hard-to-read letter. Dead Astrocade. Inside info on Zgrass. Drag Race.

Letter to Bob Fabris (Guy McLimore Jr)(Oct 29 1979).pdf - October 29, 1979.  ABC Hobbycraft. JE610 Keyboard. Distribution. Tim Hays of Seebree's Computing.  Medieval fair.  No new carts in over six months.

Enjoy the documents and have fun!

Brett is referring to this letter:

https://archive.org/stream/Bally_Astrocade_Document_Collection_Astrocast_14/Letter%20to%20Bob%20Fabris%20%28Oct%2027%201979%29%28Brett%20Bilbrey%29#mode/2up

Here is the lightly corrected, not-too-bad OCRed text (which I have not proofread) of that letter.  There are some handwritten notes on the page and a postscript which have not, of course, been proofread.

This is Brett's letter:

----------------------------------------

Dear Sir,

I am a student working at the University of Michigan in the Office of Individualized Learning. Our department deals with forms of individulized learning, such as video productions, audio tapes,and computerized devices that tutor students. It is with these computerized devices that I came in contact with the Bally.

For work purposes we required a dependable and at the time available computer system, and the TRS-80 was chosen to do what work we required. But in the comparison we included the Bally because of its projected capabilities with the add-on unit. Because Bally was not ready for production the TRS-80 won. But, I was caught!!!!

I picked up a Bally in March,but had to return it for another because of heating problems. My existing Bally is of the second run. So enough of the background. I've recieved thru a friend all of Bally's cartridges, the BASIC, and the interface. The latest cartridges are;

Panzer Attack and Red Baron
Clowns and Brickyard
Blackjack, Poker, and Acey-Deucey
(as of 10/27/78)

If you do not already have these cartridges they should be in your area soon. Also, a Star Wars cartridge is due by 11/11/78 but that means two weeks later.

The reason I am writing is I heard that you are starting a user group and would like to recieve information in exchange for what secrets that I know of the Bally and some fantastic (at least I think there are) programs written by a computer programer here at U of M. For example Life, Compucolor's cannon program-shoot, a four player laser game, and others. The way we have been able to write these programs is by commands that are not listed in the manual but are still there. Similar to the STOP, and ABS(x) commands. You may know of these but if not can we arrange an exchange of information. Also, I can directly access the music processor thru the Master Oscillator Frequency, the Vibrato System, the Noise System,and the Volume register. This lends to realistic explosions and other sounds. I also have been able to display more than two colors on the screen using BASIC and have found more graphics commands.(this is what makes the games FANTASTIC.)

I would like to make note to those interested in modifying there Ballys, the PA-1 Service Manual applies only to the first run of machines and many changes have been made. (i.e. the four ROM's have been replaced by one, and minor shifting of positions of certian parts) The changes are not much but check before making modifications.

I would like to mention an article on the Bally BASIC by one of the Prof.'s here. Dr. Zinn has written an introductory article which can be found in the Sept-Oct issue of creative computing.

I have rushed writing this letter after having found out about your group (so please forgive my typing. My printer has been out of wack and manual retyping this is frightening)

Please include myself and my friends in your user group and I'm sure that our contrabutions will be informitive and useful.

Thank you,
Brett Bilbrey
EE student

----------------------------------------

I think that Kevin Bunch will be happy to see that Brett mentioned the release date of November 11, 1978 for "the Star Wars cartridge," which was released as "Star Battle."  I'm not sure if that cartridge was releaesed on that exact day, but it's a 2K game and it's certainly among the first group of Bally Arcade cartridges.  This must be one of the very first games that steals the Trench Scene from Star Wars.

These letters that were written to the Arcadian are really a "Treasure Cove" of information.  Yeah, yeah, I mean treasure trove of information... ;-)

Adam

On Wed, Apr 29, 2020 at 11:10 AM, Adam Trionfo wrote:

> 
> Has anyone here ever used the three-voice music program to create any

Yes. 😁

I wrote the Basic/Machine Code three voice music program, and George Moses did an amazing job writing music for it. George also wrote the documentation.

For our Treasure Cove cartridge, I also wrote an ADSR routine. When you hear the "ship's bell", that is the ADSR code.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(music)

When I was in college at the University of Michigan, for one of my computer classes, I had to 'interface' with the real world. Most of the other students simulated a burglar alarm system by having an external switch wired to the I/O port. If the switch 'opened', then someone had opened a window or door, and they would set off an alarm sound. I wanted to do something a bit more interesting, so I interfaced a speaker to the computer I/O port. (The computer we were using at the time was a PET, and while it made a beep sound, it could not play music.)  I then wrote a music program that read the notes and had two loops. The first loop created the 'tone' of the note, and the second loop determined the length of the note. I then created the data to play the University of Michigan fight song. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EF--ldYIBnM
I got an A in that class... 😉

But between the Bally three voice music program, and that computer class, that was about all the music programming that I did. It was an interesting experiment for me, but I fell in love with image processing algorithms and started a company that built video boards... https://www.apollo.io/companies/Intelligent-Resources-Integrated-Systems/5b857c3b324d446a279c5de1

I even found an old ad for it... (scroll up to see the 'Video Explorer' ad)
https://books.google.com/books?id=GzwEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA28&lpg=PA28&dq=%22Intelligent+Resources+Integrated+Systems%22

The Video Explorer was the first digital video board. For the time, it was pretty cool. A bunch of other companies used the video board as the base for their own products.
" Intelligent Resources Integrated Systems'​ primary product was the Video Explorer, the first video card to bridge the computer and broadcast video industries digitally. The Video Explorer was the first computer video card to support HD video and CCIR601 digital interfaces. As to the price, the base board was $10,000
That was the price of video processing back in the day...

Hi-Res Fish Demo Update.

All the low to hi-res conversion coding is completed. The coding is set up for the motion of up to 18 fish. Whether or not the Magic RAM or possibly the Z80 can handle that much motion perfectly remains to be seen. My particular DRAM or SRAM  hi-res hardware design could impose some restrictions. I know for sure that 9 patterns can be moved around a hi-res map with no problems. This hi-res fish demo also utilizes 2 screen interrupts to split the screen horizontally, so I can add 3 more new colors to the sea bottom. Having 2 screen interrupts might create some problems writing multiple graphic patterns, I don't know. Anyway, I am soon going to begin my experimentation moving over 9 fish around a hi-res screen map.

I used Bit Fiddler's clever approach to move multiple fish around the screen using only one vector block. I came up with an idea to extend this approach for an application using multiple sizes of fish, each with its distinct vector limits table, so that the required Z80 coding would be minimized. My idea presented to you earlier, to use bit 7 in a Magic Register value as an extended flop request, to flop a pattern in the exact same pattern frame as a normal write, works great. It took me a while to figure out and come up with a routine to compute the required x coordinate adjustment for a flop. I forgot that a normal magic write shifts right and a flop write shifts left. MCM

17127:
I uploaded Astrocast #15 today, in which I conduct a user interview with David Kindred.

David got his Astrocade console in 1981 when he was eleven years old. He learned to program in Bally BASIC, which caused a spark that eventually ignited into a flame that drove David to college where he studied computer science and information technology. He worked for 25 years as a computer programmer, beginning with Fortune 500 companies, before he moved into IT management, where he works to this day.

In this podcast, David explains how using the Bally/Astrocade helped to shape his early views on programming and how the system and its BASIC programming language allowed him to be precise in his thinking. Lastly, lets not forget the fun tale of the subtle drawing of a tree with toilet paper hanging from its limbs that he created with a friend using the Astrocade's built-in program, Scribbling. Why would he draw this small wonder of art? This humble drawing glorified the cute misconduct of two thirteen year old boys who had spent the previous evening TP-ing a neighbor's tree.

If you have ever wondered what it felt like to be the owner and user of a minority game system like the Astrocade, then David can help fill in some of the blanks that are so hard to come by when talking to people who grew up with the more mainstream game systems like the Atari 2600 or much more popular computers like the Apple II.

Thanks to David for allowing me to interview him; it was fun!

You can listen to the Astrocast #15 here:

http://ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/podcast/bally-alley-astrocast-episode-15-user-interview-with-david-kindred

There are only a few show notes for this episode.  If you've never seen the Astrocade catalogs called The Soucebook, then follow that link.  You'll be surprised how much software and hardware were compiled in these manuals.

Coming soon in future Astrocast episodes:

Astrocast #16 is a going to cover part of the AstroBASIC manual.  Most of that episode is recorded too, but none of it is edited yet.

Astrocast #17 - By the time episode #17 rolls around, I hope to review Brickyard/Clowns" and WaveMakers' "Outpost 19" with Chris.  If he's not available yet, then I may review a few AstroBASIC tape releases on my own.

Astrocast #18 - Cover November 1979 issue of Arcadian and more letters from that time period.

If you would like to be interviewed for a user interview, then contact me and we'll set up a time to talk via Skype or phone.

Have fun listening to Astrocast #15!

17128:
The other day I had the opportunity to interview Nola Donato. She was involved in GRASS and ZGRASS for a while before her career took her elsewhere in the tech industry (with a few more video game-related stints with Mattel and 3DO). 
Nola started off in chemistry, but after being involved with molecular modeling with a vector display, decided she liked the computer side of things more; once the main input method shifted away from punch cards to keyboards she was all in and moved her major over to that burgeoning field. With computers being so new, undocumented and largely untouched outside of specific areas of study, one of her first tasks was to pioneer and educate students on computer graphics and how they worked - at the time, it was all vectors. This was basically how she ended up working on the original GRASS, which ran on a PDP-11 and a Vector General. The idea behind GRASS, of course, was to provide a fairly easy and powerful method for artists and graphic design folks to do what they were doing. She indicated it was a bit of a mixed result - a lot of artists aren't programmers and vice versa, but this meant that artists could have trouble grasping what the limitations of the computer would be when they were working on their designs. So what would happen is programmers would essentially set the parameters and the artists could work within that using the Vector General's rotary dials and joystick. Apparently at one point they even hosted an art show where every artist was teamed with a programmer (which she said was a difficult experience for the reasons I just outlined).
Relevant to this group, Donato was responsible for ZGRASS as the primary author! She said the differences between the original PDP-11's setup and the Bally system - display technology, processors, etc. meant that she essentially had to create the language again from scratch. Essentially no code was shared between GRASS and ZGRASS, just the basic concept. Since it was requested that it also operate like Bally BASIC on the Bally system, she was the primary author for the language aspects to make it more BASIC-esque (as opposed to being more like Assembly on the PDP). She doesn't have anything related to it anymore, unfortunately, though she was very surprised that there's a group of people interested in the language even though it never came out for the Bally system!
She left Chicago to move to California because there were more jobs in tech out there, and more fun ones as well. This led her to Mattel Electronics, where she worked on procuring advanced computers capable of simulating different proposed next gen hardware systems in their research department. Said this included low-level stuff, like seeing what a pixel addressable setup would run like vs. a sprite-based machine, etc. once the market busted she was laid off and moved into the general tech field, working on productivity software and eventually hardware components with Intel and other companies. She did have one more stint in video games with 3DO, where she worked on software for the M2 platform itself (not game software, but system software). When the M2 was sold off she was shuffled over to the game software development side before 3DO dropped the M2 platform entirely, at which point she left the company.

17132:
Here is a link to a hand-written letter by Karen Nelson to Bob Fabris that mentions Nola Donato:

https://ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#KarenNelsonLetterSeptember101979

Here is a summary of Karen's 7-page hand-written letter:

Karen is a programmer who got interested in the Bally when JS&A advertised it in Scientific American in 1977. She was told that she was one of the first people to get her hands on one. She was very excited about machines potential, but was disillusioned by the heat problems which were inherent in the first machines. She "burned out" two of the units. Just after she returned the second unit, she discovered that her programming instructor was doing the graphics for the Bally. She says, "Yes, folks, it was the infamous Tom DeFanti and his magic Z-GRASS." She knows Tom well enough to drop into his "Graphics Habitat" at the University of Chicago to talk intelligently about some of his projects. She also knows Nola Donato and a few other of Tom students who are working on projects for Bally. Tom has had the University of Chicago purchase eight Bally's and eight Sony TVs to teach students the basics of computers and programming.

In August 1979, Tom was the chairman of a traffic seminar held jointly by IEEE and ACM/SIGGRAPH. For three nights, Tom and his crew presented new and interesting works in various areas of computer graphics (including a few by people using Bally Arcades). In addition to the seminar, a graphics experiment Expo was held and it was there that Karen met some of the guys from Dave Nutting, in particular Ricky Spiece (who developed the Football cartridge). Ricky was helpful and showed Karen some tricks (like the ports in BASIC), and he also demonstrated the graphics capabilities by loading a picture from a disk to a color monitor. In addition, his Bally was connected to a B&W monitor and a keyboard. His commands appeared on the black-and-white monitor, and the graphics were displayed on the color monitor. However, the whole setup was attached with the Bally board mounted in a frame, not in the case, which leads Karen to believe that some special wiring is needed.

Karen describes her experimentation with the different ports available in BASIC.

Karen has recently seen the pinball cartridge demoed at the graphic seminar. She says that it looks pretty good. She heard one of the Dave Nutting guys say that he had just sent the thing off to Bally and that it should be out on the market pretty soon. Karen says that there was a demo of Z-GRASS, but that she didn't get to see it. She does note that as a student of De Fanti, she learned how to program in GRASS-- Z-GRASS's daddy-- using a PDP-11/45.

Karen is glad to find out that there are other people like her who think that the Bally Arcade/computer has a lot more potential than most people give it credit for. She hopes that Bob Fabris might be able to pass on some information to whoever the marketing manager at Bally is. She would like to see the Bally advertisement computer magazines such as BYTE and Personal Computing. She would like to see Bally stress that most people buy home computers for games and that Bally has terrific controls, and that by the time people become interested in programming, Bally will have add-on module available. She also says that the graphics capabilities of the Bally have no competition; they are the best, and the Arcade is dirt cheap when compared to other systems.


Just imagine if everything in the Bob Fabris Collection was keyword searchable!

Adam

I added the PA Tiny BASIC source code to BallyAlley.com about three years ago.  Now I've uploaded it to archive.org, here:

----------------------------------------

I have added Palo Alto Tiny BASIC, Version 3 by Li-Chen Wang. This article (which includes the source code and assembly listing) is excerpted from pages 58-88 of the 1977 book PCC's Reference Book of Personal And Home Computing, Edited by Dwight McCabe.  Paul gave me this book this past weekend-- so... thanks, Paul!

For those not already aware, Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC" are a superset of the original Palo Alto Tiny BASIC.

This version of Li-Chen Wang's Palo Alto Tiny BASIC will run on either the 8080 or Z-80, and only uses 2K of core memory. It contains a number of nice features including command abbreviations and error messages. At the end of the listing is a cross reference table for symbols used in the program and also the object code for the program. For further information on Tiny BASIC languages, see Dr. Dobb's Journal, Volume 1.

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#PaloAltoTinyBASIC3SourceCodepdf

I've seen various versions of the source code for Tiny BASIC, but I've never come across version 3.0 before I saw the listing in this book.  At about 2K in size, this version of Tiny BASIC is very small (well, duh!).  It's not wonder that Jay Fenton was able to expand upon this version of Tiny BASIC when he ported it to the Astrocade as a 4K cartridge.  Bally BASIC includes numerous editions to the language, including the ability to work with graphics.

I looked around for the the 8080 source code in an assembler-ready format for this version of Tiny BASIC, but I couldn't find it.

Has anyone ever compared all of the differences (and similarities) between Tiny BASIC, Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC?"

Adam

I'm interested to see how the BASIC version of "Artillery Duel" works.  Last night I made a text-readable "print out" of the BASIC code.  You are all probably aware of this game, but if not, then you can check out me and Chris (my sometimes Astrocast co-host) playing the game:

The original Bally Arcade/Astrocade BASIC version of John Perkins' Artillery Duel (first published in the May 19, 1980 issue of the Arcadian newsletter on pages 58 and 59) is compared to the 4K cartridge release of the game (part #5005) released by Astrocade Inc. as part of the Action/Skills Series in 1982.
www.youtube.com
This is a text listing of the AstroBASIC game Artillery Duel that was converted by me last night (May 11, 2020).  The conversion was created from an audio file in this archive:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#ArtilleryDuelJohnPerkinsAB

This is the specific version of the game in WAV format that was converted:

Artillery Duel (1981)(John Perkins)(2000 Baud)(PD).wav

I used BallyBin 2 to get the BASIC code from the digitally archived version of the AstroBASIC game program.

I used the following version of BallyBin to get the BASIC data:

AstroWAV and Ballybin 2 (2005)(Bob Colbert)(beta)[Dec 31 2005]

I renamed the WAV file to artduel.wav.  Then I used Ballybin with the following command line to get the BML file with the BASIC data in it:

ballybin -v2 -d1 artduel.wav

I massaged the data to make it a little more readable using Microsoft Word and ANSI characters which I inserted by holding down the Alt key and then pressing various number combinations on the number pad.  Make sure that numlock is down, or else this won't work.

I replaced the following codes that BallyBin uses:

                  Astrocade           Keyboard
BallyBin Symbol   Equivalent          Combination
---------------   ----------          -----------
|divided_by|      ÷ (Divide)          Alt+0247 - ÷ (Divide Sign)
|*|               × (Multiply)        Alt+0215 - × (Multiplication Sign)
|down_arrow|      ↓ (Down Arrow)      Alt+25   - ↓ (Down Arrow)

There are many more BallyBin-substitution words possible, but I think that "Artillery Duel" only uses two of these three Astrocade-specific symbols.

>>
If you look at Amazing Maze when it is being made, it uses a lot of screen RAM on the bottom

Yup, I know what you're talking about with RAM at the bottom of the screen.  Amazing Maze is a excellent example of "seeing" screen screen.  Normally technique is most helpful to machine code programmers.  When AstroBASIC "clears" the screen, it doesn't wipe out the bottom of the screen, which just isn't displayed to begin with in BASIC.  The bottom of the screen in BASIC holds the arrays, variables and other goodies.  If you wiped that information out, then CLEAR would be a useless command.

Adam

Yup, I know what you're talking about with RAM at the bottom of the screen.  Amazing Maze is a excellent example of "seeing" screen screen.  Normally technique is most helpful to machine code programmers.  When AstroBASIC "clears" the screen, it doesn't wipe out the bottom of the screen, which just isn't displayed to begin with in BASIC.  The bottom of the screen in BASIC holds the arrays, variables and other goodies.  If you wiped that information out, then CLEAR would be a useless command.

Hi, Allen,

The way I interpret this, I think they might be referring to a bulletin board system, or BBS. These were popular before the internet took off. You’d use your computer to connect with a BBS and, using a terminal program, be able to leave messages for other members on the same BBS and also exchange files. They were quite popular for distributing pirate software. Some BBS system operators, or sysops, formed alliances with other BBS sysops and let their BBS systems call each other at odd hours to exchange messages targeted for users on other BBS’s.

Anyone else have a different take on it?

Warmest wishes,

—David

David's take on this store seems about right.  I don't think JS&A were create a BBS, but it certainly wasn't the "Internet." Adam

I have spent several hours today continuing trying to unravel how the AstroBASIC game "Artillery Duel" works.  I talked about my work trying to document this program, and I'll continue just a bit here.

I've added my handwritten comments to the printed program.  I have several pages of 8 1/2" x 11" three-ring, college-ruled note paper filled with BASIC lines that I have written down from the program.  Sometimes I write just one line down and then try to work my mind through that line of code.  One bit that was hard to follow today was this line:

280 GOSUB 500+A×2×(A<45)+(90-A)×2×(A>40);IF A>45K=K÷100+RM×100

Wheh!  This line boils down to a jump to another section of the program, retrieves some data and then, if required, manipulates the returned data.  I figured out that A was the angle of the gun barrel.  Some statements really threw me for a curve.  For instance (A<45), (90-A) and (A>40) seem like they should not work, but they do function correctly.  These kinds of statements are Boolean logic; twisted bits of code usually used to avoid IF statements.  I've run across them before, and I'm aware of how people use Boolean logic in BASIC to shorten program and avoid IF statements, but that doesn't make them easy to use.

I did wrap my head around line 280 enough to understand that if the guns angle is set to, for example, 30°, then the program, as seen by AstroBASIC, becomes:

280 GOSUB 570; [more code]

This jumps to line 560:

560 K=8650;RETURN 

The number (K) is then broken down into X, Y coordinates.  Line 280 checks if the angle is over 45° (it isn't).  If the angle was larger, then the value of K would be swapped from "8650" to "5086."

This is probably a bit boring for most readers.  But it's a fun puzzle to me.  I've not reached a solution yet.  It's now time to gather my notes together, type them up, and see where I stand.  Then I'll take a break and continue to look at the program in a few days with fresh eyes.

I think that I have this program correctly restructured so that it's a bit easier to read.  Sometimes I get confused with how an IF statement works in AstroBASIC.  I think that if an IF statement is not true, then the entire rest of the line is skipped.  In this way, if several IF statements are on the same line, than (I THINK) it acts like an ELSE IF structure.

Now that the program is a little easier to read, I should be able to comment it a bit easier.  Also, figuring out variables becomes easier too.  For instance, it's easy to see that W = Wind. I've run across them before, and I'm aware of how people use Boolean logic in BASIC to shorten program and avoid IF statements, but that doesn't make them easy to use.

> I did wrap my head around line 280 enough to understand that if the guns angle is set to, for example, 30°, then the program, as seen by AstroBASIC, becomes:
> 
> 280 GOSUB 570; [more code]
> 
> This jumps to line 560:
> 
> 560 K=8650;RETURN 
> 
> The number (K) is then broken down into X, Y coordinates.  Line 280 checks if the angle is over 45° (it isn't).  If the angle was larger, then the value of K would be swapped from "8650" to "5086."

I'm glad that you and Lance find my small investigation into "Artillery Duel" interesting.

I find Tiny BASIC, and especially the Bally Arcade's enhanced version of Palo Alto Tiny BASIC (which was already an enhancement of the original Tiny BASIC), to be fun to dig into with some depth.  The programmer's who used Bally BASIC had some severe disadvantages, the most obvious of which is the small amount of RAM, but the the language was also interger-only, although there were some features sported by Tiny BASIC (like the Remainder "variable," RM) which allowed this shortcoming to be worked around a little bit.

I'll continue to look at "Artillery Duel," which has captured my attention recently mostly because so many Astrocade users have played it (they could type it in, after all) and yet there isn't really much written about how the program works.  I'm quite surprised that I've never come across any deep-dive into the program in all of my reading about the Astrocade, including the documentation in the Fabris Collection.

Anyway, it was one of my favorite games, so I tried programming it on the Bally Arcade.

But mine ran too slow, and it took up a LOT of code space. Why? Because I was trying to 'compute' the sin/cos values for the projectile.

Well, John was a bit smarter than me, and he figured out that he could 'pre compute' the values, and then quantize the sin/cos table, and further he could fine tune the shot with what the actual value of the knob was. John's code ran 10 times faster than mine. He taught me a wonderful lesson that I've remember the rest of my career. "Don't brute force something if you can find a clever shortcut."

So, that code that you are pondering I believe is John's look up table for which values to use to make different parabolas for the projectile.

Does that help?

280 GOSUB 500+A×2×(A<45)+(90-A)×2×(A>40);IF A>45K=K÷100+RM×100

Wheh! This line boils down to a jump to another section of the program, retrieves some data and then, if required, manipulates the returned data. I figured out that A was the angle of the gun barrel. Some statements really threw me for a curve. For instance (A<45), (90-A) and (A>40) seem like they should not work, but they do function correctly. These kinds of statements are Boolean logic; twisted bits of code usually used to avoid IF statements. I've run across them before, and I'm aware of how people use Boolean logic in BASIC to shorten program and avoid IF statements, but that doesn't make them easy to use.

Over the weekend I got to chat on the phone with Andy Guevara, known as the Bit Fiddlers fellow who wrote the Machine Language Manager, Sea Devil, Chicken, the Goldfish Demo, and Ms. Candyman (alongside the L&M guys). The audio recording from that is going to be popping up on an upcoming Astrocast, but I wanted to also provide a rundown of some of the stuff he told me:
Guevara's formal training was as an electrical engineer, doing hardware design. He was interested in the Bally game console because, as he put it, at the time game consoles were basically just small computers trying to focus in on that one area.  With that in mind, the Bally system was the most advanced unit, with distinctive graphics and sound coprocessors, and therefore he assumed it would be the most successful. Further, he already had worked with the Z80 microprocessor and had learned assembly for it, and since that chip powers the BPA, he felt he could leverage the platform to really dig into what made it tick.
Guevara got a hold of the newsletters going out at the time about the BPA, notably the Arcadian, and was able to learn a fair amount about how the machine worked; he was even able to get a copy of the system rom to dissect as well. This reverse engineering process took him "a long time," but set him up to begin writing his own software - using an Apple II Plus with a Z80-CPM card and an EPROM writing card as his development station. He also attempted to mod his sytem with additional RAM, but could never get it to work as there was a signal on the motherboard that had to be handled (and he never did).
His first program was the Machine Language Manager. This was a development cart in the same vein as Bally's own BASIC cart written by Jamie Fenton - the MLM was a way for Guevara to learn how to use the BPA keypad for data entry, and eventually he figured if he was writing this tool for his own usage, he may as well try selling it. He didn't expect there to be much of a market, and ultimately only sold about 100 carts by advertising in BPA-focused newsletters under the Bit Fiddlers name. Interestingly, the MLM was able to natively detect if the user had any hardware mods like a keyboard attachment or additional RAM - something Guevara was very pleased about! Once he'd finished the MLM he quit his day job and decided to try doing software for the Bally under the Bit Fiddlers name full time. He wrote several tutorial articles in the Arcadian newsletter on how to do machine language programming for the BPA - he explained this was essentially guerrilla marketing for him to get his name out there and drum up interest in what he was doing.  He told me that he did get some feedback from folks who were using the cart and his tutorials as part of their efforts to check their work.
With the MLM cart out, his first program using it was a simple "goldfish demo" he gave away for free. This was the first demo for the system written entirely in assembly language, allowing it to move far more smoothly and with fewer restrictions than a BASIC demo would have. The demo was little more than a digital clock, a fish tank with goldfish swimming around, and a cat watching it and meowing every minute. The goldfish demo was followed by Chicken, one of the first machine language games produced for the BPA by its enthusiast base. Chicken, as Guevara put it, was basically Frogger for all intents and purposes. You simply just had to get a chicken across the road instead of a frog. Chicken was sold on a cassette tape after Guevara had worked out a way to load the game up using Bally BASIC, though he estimates only 20-30 copies ever did get sold. Guevara chalked up poor sales in part to the system's struggles to actually get marketed (Bally  and later Astrovision did a poor job of this, he said) on top of third party games lacking that Bally/Astrovision name, and thus being perceived as more questionable.
 His second game, Ms. Candyman, was a collaboration with L&M Software, another enthusiast-led "company" selling BPA software made up of two guys, Greg Miller and Bill Loos. L&M had done an original Candyman game using a combination of BASIC and machine language routines, and wanted to pair with Guevara for a cartridge-based, all machine language sequel. Guevara said this was a great combo - while he had a lot of technical skills and smarts, he said he wasn't very strong on the creative side of things, whereas L&M were great at coming up with game ideas. Guevara designed the cartridge boards, found a cheap source of chips to put the game program on, had the cartridge molds made (he noted that it didn't occur to him until afterwards, but he could probably have just bought existing ones from Astrovision), and collaborated with L&M on the game program itself. They discussed the game mechanics, the character sprites, how characters should move (he wanted smooth motion, they wanted characters to jump around), and even the music - L&M wanted to use the then-relatively recent Candyman song, while Guevara proposed Good Ship Lollipop because it was less likely to run into legal troubles. Guevara is particularly proud of this, as he had been learning guitar at the time and was able to pick out the right musical frequencies on the BPA to get the song to sound almost exactly right on his first try. He said they essentially would work on a game and then mail a copy of it back and forth from the L&M office in Illinois and his place in California. When Ms. Candyman was released, it was well received. In a follow up email, he told me that L&M had reached out to him to add some assembler language to their games due to the limitations of Bally BASIC; he helped them put together movement routines that were much smoother. He believes that his tutorials are what made them get in touch with him in the first place.
Guevara went through L&M to publish his final game Sea Devil. This was a Defender clone, as Guevara really liked that game and wanted to try and bring it to the BPA. His initial idea was to have it be called DeBumper, and have it take place in a junkyard with you playing as a bumper, but then it occurred to him that he could do an underwater theme and have it be a little more easily recognizable. In many ways the game plays like Defender regarding the shooting aspects, but it doesn't include the rescue component of the arcade game. Guevara explained that he wanted to include it, but after six months he was tired of working on it. Trying to cram games into limited cartridge space took a lot of time and energy, he said, and while he would have liked to have "completed" the game, he was just done. L&M did the marketing for it, and while he did end up getting $700 for sold copies, he estimated that it didn't break 100 copies.
After Sea Devil, the video game market had collapsed, so he decided to go back into getting a real job. Only now he wasn't interested in hardware design, and so took up work as a programming consultant for a few years before joining a company doing laser printer software, which got him into programming full time. Guevara is still interested in video games, but not so much as a player - he finds watching others play them and appreciating the artistry that goes into the games far more engrossing. Nevertheless, he notes the BPA really changed the trajectory of his career.

Guevara does still have his original materials from his games, and did express interest in donating them to the Strong Museum - he also told me he is releasing his games into the public domain because, as he put it, they're already online so who cares. His favorite games for the system ended up being Incredible Wizard and Artillery Duel - as Adam already posted, Andy was impressed with the work John Perkins did on that, both with the BASIC and the cart versions.

From: Michael Matte
Sent: Saturday, May 23, 2020 11:57 AM
Subject: What's Up with C10?
 
The electrolytic C10 is suppose to reduce the DC ripple created by a full-wave rectifier with a resistance/capacitance load. This particular cap is used on a reverse -5vdc power supply, which only supplies a few mA, so only 100uf is needed to keep the ripple to an acceptable level. Being an electrolytic used on a neg power supply, its positive end has to be connected to the system ground. You can confirm this with a DC voltmeter. A voltmeter connected across C10 will tell which end is "more positive". What will happen to the cap if you connect it backwards? I'm not sure. It may still reduce the ripple until the cap fails. What will happen physically to it when it fails, i.e., will it "pop"?  Perhaps not. This cap is a challenge to replace because the positive end is soldered to a ground pad. Yuck. My soldering irons don't like this cap C10.

Bye.
MCM

0066-116XX-XXYX < Astrocade
0066-118XX-XXYX < WoW
2721-0066-116 < GORF

I would not use this 'RGB interface' I just made a copy for preservation's sake; I might even make a board from it.
However, I don't think the old RGB interface could compare to a modern solution.
I would rather use the LM1881 (sync stripper) and 6 op-amps. The LT6559 actually provides a YPbPr to RGB design in their datasheet.

On using the YPbPr directly; I do not know what the voltage is there.
If someone has an oscilloscope, an Astrocade, and some free time please let me know those voltages.
What I need specifically is the peak to peak voltages of Y (white to black [ignoring sync]), Pb (blue to yellow), and Pr (red to cyan).
Honestly, I am sort of stuck until I get either measurement from the community or a replacement Astrocade adapter of some sort.

Another note: The Colecovision and the Astrocade both use the LM1889 to get RF video out from YPbPr.
So I would believe any analog solution for Colecovision would be more or less the same for the Astrocade.

Please ignore any errors; I am tired. I can give more information if needed (possibly). I am not an EE so someone else feel free to step in here.

So for RGB if you want to measure P-P (which should be around 714mv) you just need to measure the difference between white (max) and black (min) on all three lines.
Max white is 714mv P-P on all thee lines on RGB. For example if you wanted to see this range you could just have a black and white checkerboard pattern.

The Astrocade and Colecovision has YPbPr which is a bit different and more complicated IMO.
I think the general range is -350mv to +350mv for Pb and Pr (so 700mv p-p) and Y is just 714mv.

So for Y its P-P can be measured the same as RGB all you need is a black and white screen.
For Pb and Pr it is different but I think that max Pr is a fully saturated red and max Pb is similarly a max saturated blue.
Pb min should be max red and max green so full saturated yellow, and Pr min should be max blue and max green so fully saturated cyan.
So a yellow and blue pattern should give Pb p-p and a cyan and red patten fro Pr p-p
For reference. ( https://i.imgur.com/oR9NVEL.png )

Now I think that is correct well enough to not put much more thought into it.

Here is what the YPbPr looked like on my colecovision:
https://i.imgur.com/ju3yVMK.png

Im using the cursor to measure the p-p on all of the lines; notice I am skipping that bump on Y since that is sync.
My measurements here are not using a color test screen or anything that is probably the start screen with no cart in that I am measuring and does not have the full scale as I'd need.

Even a rough estimate may be some progress as here I can see on the coleco that it is roughly 1v so I know it won't damage my TV.

The electrolytic C10 is suppose to reduce the DC ripple created by a full-wave rectifier with a resistance/capacitance load. This particular cap is used on a reverse -5vdc power supply, which only supplies a few mA, so only 100uf is needed to keep the ripple to an acceptable level. Being an electrolytic used on a neg power supply, its positive end has to be connected to the system ground. You can confirm this with a DC voltmeter. A voltmeter connected across C10 will tell which end is "more positive". What will happen to the cap if you connect it backwards? I'm not sure. It may still reduce the ripple until the cap fails. What will happen physically to it when it fails, i.e., will it "pop"?  Perhaps not. This cap is a challenge to replace because the positive end is soldered to a ground pad. Yuck. My soldering irons don't like this cap C10.

Bye.
MCM

The white ROM's are not uncommon.  Those seem to be the first 3159 single chip ROM and every one I have seen says 1977 on the menu screen.

Here is what I have figured out about the ROMs from working on the Bally.

1.  3164 4 chip ROM
2.  3159 4 chip ROM
3  3159 white chip ROM
4.  3159 black chip ROM - all of these seem to say 1978 on the menu.  All the other say 19887  The black chip is by far the most common of the other 3 put together, and that's not a bad thing!

If you want to see a "rare" ROM, I have one in my basement.  It's a unit I haven't gotten to work.  It's grey, and it's the only one I've ever seen.  I should pull it and put it in a socket to see what the date shows.

That whit custom you have is an address chip.  Where the "A: is in the middle line would be a "D" for data or "I" for I/O.  I've seen all 3 before, but NOT ALL IN ONE UNIT.  I'll try to get you the pics sent later today.

----------------------------------------

It might be a good idea to start keeping track of when the custom chips in each unit were made.  The earliest I've seen from an Astrocade are from 1977.  The latest are from 1981.  I suppose the custom chips used in the arcade units might have been made further into the 1980s.

In episode #16 of the Bally Alley Astrocast, Kevin Bunch interviews Andy Guevara. The interview took place Saturday, May 16, 2020. Andy wrote three programs that were released on cartridge for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade. The first cartridge was Machine Language Manager (MLM), released by The Bit Fiddlers in 1982. L&M Software approached Andy due to his machine language skills and a collaboration got underway that produced Ms. Candyman and Sea Devil, which were both released on cartridge in 1983. Andy also wrote some additional software: Chicken and the Goldfish Demo were released on tape, while a few others were released as type-in programs. Mr. Guevara's used an Apple II Plus with a Z80 card which ran the CP/M operating system to write most of his software for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.
